paras: The killing of Robert Taylor took place on the afternoon of March 1, 1882, when James Byrne, an officer of the Maryland penitentiary in Baltimore, shot dead Taylor, a Black convict, in the prison foundry. A coroner's jury ruled the same day that Byrne had acted in self-defense, and the story ran in short wire items as the shooting of an insubordinate convict.

Taylor, described as "colored" and from Somerset County, worked in the penitentiary foundry. According to the Baltimore Sun's account, reprinted in Richmond, foreman George W. Thorn had reported him the day before for spoiled work, and Warden Wilkinson had reprimanded him and ordered him to redo it after finishing the next day's task.

At about 1:45 p.m. on Wednesday, Thorn ordered Taylor to do the work over, and when Taylor neither moved nor answered, Byrne repeated the order. One Baltimore dispatch said Taylor replied that he would not go to the other floor and then assaulted Byrne, who fired. In the Sun's fuller version, Taylor said "something about getting into trouble," seized a molder's rammer and struck at Byrne just as the officer drew his pistol, and the blow discharged the pistol and knocked it from Byrne's hand.

The foreman then grabbed or separated the two men, and Taylor broke free. A convict handed the pistol back to Byrne, who fired two more shots, and Taylor fell mortally wounded. One dispatch said he died within an hour, another that he was killed almost instantly.

A jury of inquest found that Taylor was killed by balls from Byrne's pistol and that the shooting was done in self-defence, "according to the order of his superiors," and was justifiable. No report of an arrest or any later proceeding against Byrne appears in the coverage.

Two differently worded Baltimore dispatches went out on March 1: one, printed by the National Republican in Washington and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, gave a step-by-step account, while the other, carried in New Haven and Wilmington, described a "murderous onslaught" with "a heavy billet of wood." Headlines ranged from the neutral "Shot and Killed in Prison" and "A Keeper Kills a Convict" to the New Haven paper's "A Murderous Convict Shot Down." The Richmond Daily Dispatch reprinted the Sun's long account under the headline "Tragedy in a Penitentiary. Shooting of an Insubordinate Convict by a Guard in Maryland."

Washington and Maryland papers reduced the story to a sentence or two, saying Taylor was shot "for insubordination" or by an officer "whom he had assaulted." A Virginia weekly repeated it on March 11 in a news summary, calling the shooting self-defense after "a desperate attack on the keeper." Every account came from the prison side, the papers printed it as fact, and one described Taylor as "a powerful man, and at times very hard to manage."

The accounts differ on details: Taylor's weapon was a molder's rammer according to the Sun and a Maryland brief, but a heavy billet of wood in the other dispatch. The Sun said the first shot went off when the rammer struck Byrne's arm, while one dispatch said Byrne fired after being assaulted and another said he fired three times when hard pressed.

reader.title: Killing of Robert Taylor in the Maryland Penitentiary
bases: A prison officer, James Byrne, shot and killed a Black convict inside the Maryland penitentiary; no mob or crowd was involved (A1, A6).

Two differently worded Baltimore dispatches (A1, A2) and a fuller Baltimore Sun account (A6) agree that officer Byrne shot Taylor dead in the penitentiary on March 1 and that a coroner's jury called it self-defense, though all rest on the prison's version.

accounts.label: Baltimore wire report (version 1)
accounts.gist: Taylor refused to go to another floor to remake a casting he had destroyed and assaulted Byrne, who fired; foreman Thorne separated them, Taylor went after Thorne, then returned to Byrne, who fired twice more; Taylor died within an hour.

accounts.label: Baltimore wire report (version 2)
accounts.gist: Taylor refused orders, seized a heavy billet of wood and made a 'murderous onslaught' on Byrnes, who when hard pressed fired three times, killing him almost instantly.

accounts.label: Baltimore Sun account
accounts.gist: After a warden's reprimand for spoiled work, Taylor silently refused repeated orders, then struck at Byrne with a molder's rammer as Byrne drew his pistol; the blow discharged and knocked away the pistol, a convict handed it back, and Byrne fired two more shots.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Found the shooting done in self-defence and on his superiors' order, and justifiable.

framing.detail: The New Haven headline 'A Murderous Convict Shot Down' and the Richmond headline 'Shooting of an Insubordinate Convict' adopted the prison's account, describing Taylor's 'murderous onslaught'.
Washington, Lancaster and Wilmington papers ran one of the two Baltimore dispatches under neutral heads such as 'Shot and Killed in Prison' and 'A Keeper Kills a Convict'.
Maryland and Washington briefs reduced the story to one line: a convict shot 'for insubordination', the jury calling it self-defense.
